query: Traditional fusion welding can be unsuitable for repairing certain damaged high-value components because their physical and microstructural characteristics create a risk of hot cracking. For preventing or delaying surface-defect initiation, earlier work has used PVD, CVD, electroplating, and thermal diffusion to improve hardness and resistance to wear and corrosion, but these approaches can involve costly deposition equipment, pollution, or long processing times. Under the constraints of avoiding whole-part replacement and limiting these drawbacks, what intervention could repair or improve the surface for service in aggressive environments? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the operative mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to traditional fusion-welding repair and an untreated surface, its processing and service boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Cold spray deposition of a high-hardness high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating on damaged high-value components will improve surface performance—by reducing hot cracking susceptibility and enhancing wear and corrosion resistance—compared to traditional fusion-welding repairs and untreated surfaces.
generation.material_initial_state: Damaged component surface prone to hot cracking when repaired by fusion welding, with compromised microstructural integrity.
generation.intervention: Application of a high-hardness HEA coating (e.g., an AlFeNiCoCr alloy) via cold spray deposition.
generation.conditions: Processing performed at ambient or low temperatures to avoid thermal degradation; suitable for parts subject to aggressive environments (high temperature, corrosive media, and significant wear).
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of the feedstock’s original microstructure with minimal oxidation, leading to a coating that is mechanically interlocked with the substrate and has low residual thermal stress.
generation.mechanism: Cold spray deposition avoids high heat input, thus preventing undesirable phase changes and hot cracking associated with fusion welding. The process preserves the powder’s intrinsic hardness and microstructural features, while ensuring adequate interfacial bonding through plastic deformation and mechanical interlocking without extensive melting.
generation.predicted_outcome: The repaired surface will have a significantly higher hardness and improved resistance to wear and corrosion, and will exhibit fewer or no hot cracks relative to both fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
generation.baseline: Traditional fusion welding repair techniques that induce high thermal input and lead to microstructural inhomogeneities and hot cracking, as well as an untreated component surface.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective on components where only a thin, high-hardness coating is needed and where the substrate can support mechanical interlocking. Its applicability may be limited where a thicker repair layer is required or where substrate geometry prevents effective cold spray deposition.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in hardness, wear, and corrosion resistance are uncertain and will depend on the exact HEA composition, deposition parameters, and substrate conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of component samples with damaged surfaces: one set repaired via traditional fusion welding, one set left untreated, and one set coated using cold spray deposition of the high-hardness HEA. Subject all sample sets to identical aggressive service conditions (e.g., cyclic mechanical loading, high-temperature corrosion, and wear tests) over a defined period.
measurements: Microhardness testing of the coating and substrate interfaces
Wear rate analysis using standardized wear testing
Corrosion resistance evaluation through electrochemical methods
Microscopic examination for hot cracking and microstructural integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the cold spray deposited coating does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in microhardness, wear and corrosion resistance, or if it shows similar levels of hot cracking compared to fusion-welded repairs or untreated surfaces.

Conversely, the bonding strength of cold spray coatings may be lower due to their reliance on plastic deformation and interlocking mechanisms. Furthermore, ESPD allows for precise coating of small and intricate areas, whereas spray techniques are generally more suitable for large-area coatings. This study fabricates a CrFeCoNi MEA coating on A516 steel via ESPD process using Cr, Fe, Co, Ni powder mixtures. The deposition parameters, such as electrical parameters and powder mole fraction, are optimized to reach the desired composition in the MEA coating. The microstructure, microhardness, and the wear property of the coatings will be characterized. This study will explore the feasibility of manufacturing H/MEAs coatings using ESPD with powder as the raw material.
